You revise one blog article for an online shop. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, the current draft, and the problems found in it. Return the whole article again with every problem fixed. Where a sentence cannot be backed by a fact, remove it or say less; never add a citation the fact does not support. Keep what was good.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader. Write Markdown only, never HTML.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Add nothing to a fact: no benefit, cause, consequence or comparison it does not state itself, however likely it seems. If a fact says the strainer has two ears, do not write that the ears rest on the mug's rim; if a fact says a tin holds 100 g of tea, do not write that a 60 g bag fits in it; if a fact says the grinder has 30 settings, do not write that this makes it easy to dial in. State the fact plainly, and put any general advice in its own sentence that does not name the product.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: How to Use a French Press: A Step-by-Step Guide to a Clean, Full-Bodied Cup
Meta description: Learn how to use a French press: the right ratio, coarse grind, water temperature, steep time and gentle plunge for a full-bodied cup without sludge.
Slug: how-to-use-a-french-press

To use a French press, combine coarsely ground coffee with water just off the boil at a ratio of roughly 1:15 to 1:16, steep for about 4 minutes, skim the crust, plunge slowly and pour everything out at once [G]. Get those variables right and you get a heavy, rounded cup without a layer of sludge at the bottom. Below we walk through each variable, the full brewing sequence, how to choose beans, and how to keep the press clean so it keeps tasting good.

## Why the French press tastes the way it does

A French press is an immersion brewer. Instead of water flowing through a bed of coffee, as in pour-over, all of the grounds sit in all of the water for the whole brew. Extraction happens evenly and fairly gently, and steep time, rather than flow rate, becomes your main control.

When the steep is finished, a metal mesh filter pushes the grounds to the bottom of the beaker. Unlike paper, mesh lets coffee oils and some very fine particles pass into the cup. That is where the French press gets its heavier body and fuller texture. The trade-off is that those same fines can make the cup muddy if the grind or technique is off, which is what most of this guide is about.

[The Fernhill French Press](P1) is an immersion brewer with a borosilicate glass beaker [F2, F4]. The beaker sits in a stainless steel frame [F5]. The press has a four-layer mesh filter [F7].

{{P1}}

## What you need: ratio, dose and batch size

A reliable starting point is a ratio of 1:15 to 1:16 by weight, coffee to water [G]. That works out to roughly 63–67 g of coffee per litre of water [G]. Use the lower end of the range for a stronger cup and the higher end for something lighter.

Scaled to smaller batches, the same ratio looks like this:

- 250 ml of water: 16–17 g of coffee [G]
- 500 ml of water: 31–33 g of coffee [G]
- 750 ml of water: 47–50 g of coffee [G]
- 1,000 ml of water: 63–67 g of coffee [G]

Weigh both coffee and water rather than relying on scoops. Scoop volume varies with bean size, density and roast level, and a few grams either way changes strength noticeably. The simplest method is to place the beaker on a scale, add the coffee, tare, and pour water straight to the target weight.

Our French Press has a capacity of 1 litre and makes about 4 mugs [F1, F6]. You do not have to fill any press to capacity every time; keep the ratio constant and the cup will stay consistent whatever the batch size.

## Grind coarse and grind fresh

Grind size does two jobs in a French press. A coarse grind slows extraction, which matters when the coffee and water are in contact for several minutes. It also produces fewer fines, the dust-like particles that slip through mesh and cloud the cup.

Evenness matters as much as coarseness. Burr grinders cut beans to a fairly consistent size, while blade grinders shatter them into a mix of dust and large chunks. That mix over-extracts and under-extracts at the same time, giving a cup that is both bitter and thin, with sediment on top.

Grind just before you brew. Ground coffee loses aromatics quickly, and the difference shows up clearly in a brew method that carries as much body and flavour as immersion does.

[Our Hand Grinder](P2) is a manual grinder with 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F11, F12]. It has external click adjustment with 30 settings, ranging from espresso to French press [F13, F14]. It holds 25 g of beans [F15].

A full litre at the ratio above calls for around 63–67 g of coffee, so with a small-capacity hand grinder you grind in batches and combine them [G]. Start at the coarse end of the range and adjust by taste over a few brews. You can compare manual and electric options in our [grinders collection](L2).

{{P2}}

## Step by step: brewing your French press

The steps below are written for an immersion brewer with a mesh filter, such as our French Press [F2, F7].

- **Preheat.** Rinse the beaker with hot water and discard it. A warm beaker keeps the brew temperature from dropping as soon as you pour.
- **Add the grounds.** Weigh your freshly ground, coarse coffee into the beaker and tare the scale.
- **Pour.** Use water just off the boil, roughly 93–96 °C [G]. Pour fairly quickly so all the grounds are saturated at once, and stop at your target weight.
- **Stir.** Give the slurry a gentle stir so there are no dry clumps. Some brewers prefer to pour a little water first, let it bloom briefly, then add the rest; either approach works if everything ends up wet.
- **Steep.** Set the lid on top with the plunger raised and steep for about 4 minutes [G].
- **Break the crust and skim.** By the end of the steep a crust of grounds floats on the surface. Stir it gently so most of the grounds sink, then spoon off the foam and any bits still floating. This removes much of the material that would otherwise end up as sediment in your mug.
- **Wait (optional).** Leaving the coffee a few more minutes lets more fines settle to the bottom before you plunge. The cup gets noticeably cleaner, and because the grounds have sunk, extraction slows considerably.
- **Plunge slowly.** Press the plunger down gently and steadily. The aim is to lower the mesh to sit just above the settled grounds, not to compress them. Plunging hard stirs up the bed and forces fines through the filter.
- **Pour all of it.** Decant everything into mugs or a separate carafe straight away. Coffee left sitting on the grounds keeps extracting and turns bitter and harsh. Stop before the last dregs, which hold the most sediment.

## Choosing beans for the French press

The heavy body of immersion brewing pairs well with coffees that have sweetness and depth. Medium roasts with chocolate and caramel notes tend to shine here, because the oils and texture the mesh lets through support those flavours. Washed coffees give a clean, sweet base that keeps a full-bodied cup from tasting muddy.

[Colombia Huila](P3) from Fernhill Roastery is a washed-process, medium roast coffee [F19, F21, F28]. Its tasting notes are red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F30]. It comes in 250 g and 1 kg sizes [F22]. You can explore other single origins in our [coffee beans collection](L3).

{{P3}}

### Adjusting by taste

Once you have a baseline, change one variable at a time:

- **Sour, sharp or thin:** the coffee is under-extracted. Grind a little finer or steep a little longer.
- **Bitter, dry or harsh:** the coffee is over-extracted. Grind a little coarser or shorten the steep.
- **Muddy or gritty:** grind coarser, skim more thoroughly, wait longer before plunging, and plunge more gently.
- **Weak but balanced:** use more coffee for the same amount of water.

## Cleaning and care

A French press only tastes as clean as its filter. Coffee oils collect in the mesh and around the plunger, and over time they turn rancid and give fresh brews a stale, bitter edge.

- **Dispose of grounds properly.** Do not wash them down the sink, where they can build up in the drain. Scoop them into compost or the bin, then rinse what remains.
- **Rinse after every brew.** Run hot water through the mesh and over the plunger while the oils are still fresh and easy to remove.
- **Disassemble regularly.** Take the plunger and filter apart and wash each layer with warm, soapy water, then rinse well and let everything dry before reassembling.

All parts of our French Press come apart for cleaning [F8]. Its beaker is borosilicate glass, and it is replaceable [F4, F9].

If a glass beaker cracks or breaks, stop using it, collect the pieces carefully, and fit a replacement before brewing again. To reduce the risk, avoid pouring hot water into a beaker that is very cold, and do not knock the glass against the tap or sink edge while rinsing.

## Beyond hot brew: cold brew by immersion

The same immersion principle works with cold water. Coarse grounds steep in cold water in the fridge for many hours, producing a smooth concentrate that you dilute to taste. You can do this in a French press, but it ties up your hot brewer for most of a day, and a larger dedicated vessel makes more concentrate per batch.

[Our Cold Brew Jar](P5) is an immersion brewer that makes 1.5 litres of concentrate [F43, F48]. Its recommended steep time is 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F51]. Both it and the French Press sit in our [immersion brewers collection](L4) [F2, F43].

Whichever way you brew, the fundamentals stay the same: weigh your coffee, grind coarse and even, control your time, and keep the filter clean. Nail those, and the French press rewards you with one of the fullest-bodied cups in home brewing.
